job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts around nine at the desk I share with my grandmother's sewing machine, in the front room. I use an AI assistant for everything: drafting cover letters, debugging, rehearsing interview questions out loud. Then I work on an open-source tool for tenants' groups, which keeps me sharp and gives me something real to show. I graduated in software engineering eight months ago, top of my year, with internships at a payments start-up and a city council's digital team. My dad drives a taxi and my mum works in a school office, so I'm the first in the family with a degree and there's quite a lot riding on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then. A calmer ride. But I'd add that hype or not, I use these tools daily and I'm quicker because of them. Online I'd probably post a thread about using them well rather than arguing about the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the market is slow, but that gives me time to stand out. A lot of graduates are still waiting, and many aren't using the tools. I've done 70 applications and had five interviews, so I'm in the room at least. What worries me is the rent my parents quietly cover and the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shipping the tenants' tool and invite two co-maintainers, because recruiters look at commit history. I'd apply to the council's digital team again and to social-enterprise firms. I'd also do a few freelance jobs, like fixing small business sites, for about two hundred a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A bit restless, but nothing I can't handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're in the room at interviews. What's the missing piece?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually it's the experience requirement. Firms ask for two years for a junior job, which is absurd. I think firms should be required to hire and train, and the state should fund early-career roles, like apprenticeships but for desk jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family see the waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad says take any job, even driving. Mum says be patient. My grandmother just asks if I've eaten. It's loving, but I feel the weight of being the first one with a degree, and I don't want to let them down.

I'd tell friends to build **public work** while waiting.
think: The slow market gives me **time** to stand out, since many graduates still avoid the tools.
I feel the **weight** of being the first in my family with a degree.
do: Keep shipping the **tenants' tool** and invite two co-maintainers.
Reapply to the **council digital team** and social-enterprise firms.
Take **freelance jobs** fixing small business sites for about two hundred each.
feel: Okay, a bit **restless**, but nothing I can't handle.

steps.text: Keep shipping the tenants' tool and invite two co-maintainers
Reapply to the council's digital team and social-enterprise firms
Fix small business websites for about two hundred pounds each

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where it gets real, and I'm not scared of it, but I'd be honest that it won't be fair. Some firms will use it to cut junior roles, and others will use it to grow. I'd tell friends to learn how to direct the tools, not just copy from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Junior coding, the exact job I've applied for, is the thing most exposed. A senior developer with an assistant now does the work of a small team. That means fewer entry roles, but they'd be different, with more review and more talking to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retool: build things with the assistant, test them hard and write about it. I'd move my freelancing toward automation for small firms, like invoice sorting and booking, which they can't afford to hire for. And I'd apply to firms that are growing because of the tools, not shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a little worry underneath. I'd say it's like surfing: exciting, and a bit dangerous if you wipe out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it won't be fair. Fair to whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To people who don't have my advantage. My cousin works in customer service and his firm is moving to chatbots. He didn't have anyone showing him the tools. I'd want worker co-ops and public training so people can share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the entry roles don't appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I build my own. I'd start a small co-op with two other graduates and sell automation to local shops. It's not safe, but I'd rather be exposed doing something than waiting for a hiring manager.

say: I'd say the change is **real** but unfair, and graduates should learn to direct the tools.
I'd push for **worker co-ops** and public training so gains are shared.
think: Junior coding is the **most exposed** job, but the new roles will be about review and customers.
My cousin's move to **chatbots** shows who gets hurt without help.
do: Build projects with an AI assistant, test them hard and **write about it**.
Move my freelancing toward **automation** for small firms, like invoice sorting.
Apply to firms **growing** because of the tools.
feel: **Energised**, with some worry underneath, like surfing a big wave.

steps.text: Build and publish three projects made with an AI assistant
Sell invoice and booking automation to five local shops
Use AI agents to run the shops' routine admin
Help set up a worker co-op for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a sprint. I'd say the rules aren't ready, and I'd say it loudly, but I'd also say don't freeze. I'd ask the government for a basic income pilot and ask firms to share the gains with workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI can do any thinking job better and cheaper, then my degree stops being a ticket. What's left is owning something or doing hands-on work. I'd have two years of full thinking-AI before robots catch up around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move quickly. First, a job at any firm that will have me, to bank some pay. Second, put my freelance clients on monthly retainers. Third, I'd start learning a hands-on skill, maybe solar installation, because that holds until about 2031. And I'd talk to my dad about his taxi, since self-driving is a thinking-and-robot problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fast heartbeat. Excited by the chance and sick about my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your dad's taxi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that scares me. He has 12 years left of work and a car loan. If self-driving is part of the three-year robot delay, he gets until about 2031, and he'd get angry if I said it. I'd save as much as I could to help him re-plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the tools every day in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd use them to protect others, not just myself. I'd teach my dad and my cousin the basics. If I'm sharing the gains, then I'd rather be part of the solution than just a lucky one.

say: I'd say the rules aren't ready, but **don't freeze**, and ask for a basic income pilot.
I'd ask firms to **share the gains** with workers.
think: My degree stops being a **ticket**; what's left is owning something or hands-on work.

do: Take a **first job** anywhere to bank pay while the market lasts.
Learn **solar installation** as a hands-on skill that holds until about 2031.
feel: **Excited** by the chance and sick about my family's exposure.
S2.quote: I'd rather be part of the solution than just a lucky one.

steps.text: Take the first job offered to bank pay while hiring lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to prepare, but not to relax. I'd tell friends to keep shipping real work, and I'd argue online for retraining credits for everyone, paid for by the biggest AI firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My read is that thinking jobs go first and the rest follow, so I'd want to hold something that survives both. A cooperative that owns the automation would. I'd have five years to build one and know what's on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a role at a mid-size firm and learn how a real company runs. Then in year two I'd start the co-op on the side with two friends from my course. I'd also put savings into a low-cost index fund, because I'd want to own a piece of the thing that's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and focused. I like having a clear deadline, which is odd, but it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a co-op rather than a regular business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather workers owned the tools than rented them. I've seen small shops get squeezed by software subscriptions. If the people doing the work share ownership, the gains stay with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in your plan if things went faster than five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the mid-size firm and go straight to the co-op. I'd also double the freelancing. The firm job is a safe harbour, but if the clock speeds up I'd rather be building.

say: I'd argue for **retraining credits** paid by the biggest AI firms.
I'd tell friends to keep shipping **real work** and not relax.
think: I want something that survives both waves, and a **co-op** that owns the automation could.
Five years is enough to prepare, but not to **relax**.

Start the **co-op** on the side in year two with two friends.
Put savings into a low-cost **index fund**.
feel: **Calm and focused**, helped by a clear deadline.
S3.quote: I'd rather workers owned the tools than rented them.
fieldNote: Umar's **ownership** idea runs through every answer: workers should own the tools.
He has a clear plan with a **fallback** if time speeds up.

steps.text: Take a role at a mid-size firm and learn how it runs

Put a fixed monthly sum into a low-cost index fund
Found a worker-owned co-op for local automation work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds comfortable and I'd say that's the trap. I'd tell friends to treat it as five, since the tools will keep improving. Online I'd write about using the decade for training funds and bargaining rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. A decade lets me get a proper career going, build savings and help my parents. My worry is the first year, until a first job comes. After that I'd be rebuilding my skills every two years, which I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd land a job in the next year, probably through the council's digital team, where I interned. I'd move out with a friend within two years and help pay off my parents' car loan. I'd keep doing the open-source work and maybe teach a night class for adults who want to learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Peaceful, with a bit of excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you spend your first pay cheque?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my grandmother's hearing aids, which she's put off for a year. Then a month's rent in advance for my own place. After that, probably a good chair, because I've been sitting on a kitchen stool for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not getting a first job, mostly. Ten years of runway means little if no one hires me in year one. And my dad's taxi work could dry up faster than the rest of us expect.

say: I'd say ten years is a **trap** if people treat it as comfortable.
I'd write online about **training funds** and bargaining rights.
think: I'd be fine; the real worry is the **first year**, until a job comes.
I like the idea of rebuilding my skills every **two years**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly because of my dad. I can reinvent myself in a year, but a man of 50 with a taxi loan can't. What would help is public training for older workers, a basic income pilot and firms that share the gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not as unbothered as I sound. I like the tools, I like the challenge, but I'm very aware that I have the luck of being young and curious. A lot of people don't, and I don't want to build a career on that gap.

headlineQuote: I'm very aware that I have the luck of being young and curious.
portrait: Umar is a 23-year-old **software engineering** graduate, top of his year, living with his parents and grandmother and using AI every day.
He has done 70 applications and five interviews, with family quietly covering **rent** and a student loan to repay.
He leans left and wants worker **co-ops**, public training and shared gains, and he blames hiring rules more than technology.
He moves fast: freelance work, an open-source tenants' tool and a plan to start a **co-op** if entry roles vanish.
His biggest fear is for his father's **taxi** work; he is calm about himself but not about his family.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries him most because his father's taxi and car loan would be hit with no time.
whatWouldHelp: He wants public training for **older workers**, a basic income pilot and firms that share the gains.
